info.name: Brainixa - Reports, Ratings, Homework targeting & Pricing (update-11..15)
info.description:
Everything added or changed since the store batch, written by hand because the interesting part is not the field list.

**Order matters in two places.** Under *Base currency*, send 1 then 2 then 3 - step 3 is destructive and cannot be undone by changing the currency back. Under *Class ratings*, a student can only rate a class the attendance register says they attended, so `student/sessions/ratable` is where the valid `session_id` and `occurrence_date` come from.

**Everything returns HTTP 200**, including failures. Branch on `status` in the body, never on the HTTP code. A third value exists: `severity: "warning"` means the write SUCCEEDED but could not do everything asked of it.

Fill `date_from`, `date_to`, `occurrence_date` and `homework_id` in the environment, or let the date range default to the last 30 days.

item.name: Attendance reports
item.description:
Every live class has been writing attendance for both sides for a long time - the students in `session_attendance`, the teacher in `teacher_session_attendance`, which is what the wallet's earnings and deductions are computed from. The admin could read none of it: the only attendance endpoint was the list of EXCEPTION requests, which is the excuses rather than the attendance.

Nothing here writes, and none of it needed a migration - the data was always being recorded.

The figures come from the attendance ROWS, not from the weekly `class_sessions` template. The template says a class is meant to happen on Mondays; the rows say what happened. `present` and `late` both count as attendance; only `absent` does not.

item.name: Class ratings
item.description:
A rating for ONE live class, left by a student who was in it.

`teacher_ratings` and `course_ratings` already existed and neither can answer this, because neither has a session in it: a student rates their teacher once and that single number has to stand for a whole term. It cannot say that last Tuesday went badly.

What is rated is one OCCURRENCE. `class_sessions` is a weekly template, so the key is (session_id, occurrence_date, student_id) - the SAME pair the attendance tables use, which is what makes "did this student attend the class they rated" a join rather than a guess.

Needs migration 125, which is applied. Before it ran these answered with nothing rather than failing.

item.name: Homework targeting
item.description:
Homework aimed at particular students.

A homework row carried a subject and nothing else, so publishing one handed it to every student subscribed to that subject. A teacher wanting to set extra practice for the three students who are behind had no way to say so.

  * NO students chosen -> the homework is for everyone subscribed to the subject. This is exactly the old behaviour, and it is what every homework that already exists still does.
  * students chosen -> only they see it, and only they may submit to it.

Targeting NARROWS an audience and never widens one: a student still has to be subscribed to the subject, so no row here hands anyone access they did not already have.

Wire-level: `student_ids`, `students` and `is_targeted` are ADDED to the homework object. Nothing was removed or renamed, and a client ignoring all three behaves exactly as before.

Needs migration 126, which is applied.

item.name: Who a homework in this subject would reach

request.description:
The list to pick from when aiming a homework at only some students.

One aggregate query mirroring the paths a subscription can grant a subject by: the subject named directly, a course that belongs to it, or a teacher who teaches it - each arriving either on the subscription or on the subscription code behind it.

It is a PICKER, NOT AN AUTHORITY. The save path re-checks the handful actually chosen against the real access function and warns about any who cannot see the subject, so a name this list gets wrong is caught there rather than quietly acted on.

Identical answer - it is the subject's audience, which does not depend on who is asking.

Permission: `manage_homework`.

With `student_ids`, only those students are shown it and only they may submit to it.

A student who turns out not to be subscribed to the subject comes back as a WARNING on an otherwise successful save (`severity: "warning"`, plus `not_eligible`) rather than failing the whole request - the homework was saved, and failing over one lapsed subscription would throw away work that was just typed.

item.name: Edit - hand it back to the whole subject

request.description:
An EMPTY `student_ids` clears the targeting, so "for everyone" is reachable from the form and not only at creation time.

Omitting the key entirely leaves the audience alone - which is what keeps an older client editing a title from silently republishing a targeted homework to the whole subject.

A multipart request (one with a file attached) cannot send an empty array at all, so a plain string is accepted too: `""` to clear, or `"3,7,12"`.

Untargeted homework in the student's subjects, PLUS homework aimed at them. Homework aimed at other people is filtered out.

The submit endpoint re-checks the same thing, so a homework this student was never shown does not become submittable because its id was guessed or kept from an older response.

item.name: Pricing by country
item.description:
WHERE THE REQUEST COMES FROM decides the price.

The country saved on the student used to beat both live signals, so a student connecting from Germany kept being quoted the base price - `source` came back as `student` and nothing about the connection could outrank it.

`students.country_id` cannot carry that weight: it holds what registration captured, what the student later chose, and what an earlier geo-IP lookup wrote into it, and once written the three are indistinguishable.

Order now: explicit `country=` -> CDN header -> geo-IP -> the saved country -> base currency.

item.name: Which country am I being priced as?

query.description: Force a country - the switcher. Beats everything else.

request.description:
WHERE THE REQUEST COMES FROM decides the price.

The country saved on the student used to beat both live signals, so a student connecting from Germany kept being quoted the base price - `source` came back as `student` and nothing about the connection could outrank it.

`students.country_id` cannot carry that weight: it holds what registration captured, what the student later chose, and what an earlier geo-IP lookup wrote into it, and once written the three are indistinguishable.

Order now: explicit `country=` -> CDN header -> geo-IP -> the saved country -> base currency.

THE FIRST THING TO CHECK when a price looks wrong. `source` tells you which rule answered: `client`, `edge`, `geoip`, `student` or `base`.

Send no token to see what an anonymous visitor gets; send `{{student_token}}` to see what a signed-in one gets.
Before the fix this answered `source: student` no matter where the request came from. It should now answer `edge` or `geoip`, and fall back to `student` only when neither could place the connection.

item.name: Pretend to be in Germany (CDN header)

request.description:
How to test the fix without a VPN. `CF-IPCountry` is what Cloudflare sends; the code also reads the Vercel, App Engine and Fastly equivalents.

Expect `iso2: DE`, `EUR`, and `source: edge`.

item.name: A listing, priced for one country

query.description: ISO2. Try DE, SA, AE, EG.
High enough to find the item you priced.

request.description:
`country=` forces the country, which is the quickest way to see the rule working.

On each row: `price` is the number to show, `currency` what it is in, `base_price` what it costs in the base currency, and `is_country_price` whether a country price was found at all.

With no country price the row falls back to the base price IN THE BASE CURRENCY - never the base number relabelled with the local currency.

item.name: Admin - country prices on one item

request.description:
What is actually stored, which is the other half of any "the price is wrong" question.

`item_type` is `course` or `book`. Packages are courses with `kind = 'package'`, so they use `course` here.

item.name: Teacher - country prices on a course I OWN

query.description: A course THIS teacher owns - from GET /teacher/courses.

request.description:
The same screen for a teacher, with an ownership check in front of it.

**`item_id` must be a course this teacher owns**, or the answer is `status: "error"` with "العنصر ده مش موجود" - verified against the live API: a teacher asking about someone else's course gets that, and asking about their own gets the prices. The message says NOT FOUND rather than NOT YOURS on purpose; whether a course exists is not a teacher's business to learn by probing ids.

So get the id from `GET /teacher/courses` rather than from the admin's list.

Note that country pricing is READ only on the student side - no teacher endpoint applies it. A teacher always sees their own base price as entered, which is the point: they set the number, they are not being quoted it.

item.name: Base currency
item.description:
Moving the base currency can no longer reprice the platform in silence.

`courses.price` and `course_books.price` are BARE NUMBERS. Nothing on the row says which currency they are in - the answer is whatever `base_currency` says today. So changing that setting converted nothing: a course priced at 300 EGP became a course priced at 300 SAR, roughly eight times dearer, with no edit and nothing on screen to show it. Setting the currency back does not undo it, because the figures were never changed.

A price reaches the incoming currency one of two ways and no third: it was already entered for a country using that currency, or the admin typed it. Anything still without one REFUSES THE WHOLE CHANGE, and nothing is written - not the prices, not the setting.

No conversion is ever invented. An exchange rate picked by the server would put a number in front of a customer that nobody approved.

query.description: The code being moved to. Must be an ACTIVE currency.

request.description:
Moving the base currency can no longer reprice the platform in silence.

`courses.price` and `course_books.price` are BARE NUMBERS. Nothing on the row says which currency they are in - the answer is whatever `base_currency` says today. So changing that setting converted nothing: a course priced at 300 EGP became a course priced at 300 SAR, roughly eight times dearer, with no edit and nothing on screen to show it. Setting the currency back does not undo it, because the figures were never changed.

A price reaches the incoming currency one of two ways and no third: it was already entered for a country using that currency, or the admin typed it. Anything still without one REFUSES THE WHOLE CHANGE, and nothing is written - not the prices, not the setting.

No conversion is ever invented. An exchange rate picked by the server would put a number in front of a customer that nobody approved.

Read-only. Returns `adoptable` (items with a stored price in the target currency, each with `current_price` and `new_price`), `missing` (items with none), `missing_by_kind`, and both counts.

Matching is on the CURRENCY, not on one country - several countries share a currency. Where more than one price exists the LOWEST is taken, because over-charging is the worse of the two mistakes.

item.name: 2. Try it with no prices - REFUSED

request.description:
What happens when the items in `missing` have not been given prices: `status: "error"`, `base_currency_blocked` naming them, and NOTHING WRITTEN. The platform is left exactly as it was.

The guard lives inside the settings endpoint rather than behind its own, precisely because a separate endpoint is what would be stepped around by posting the key straight to this one.

SAFE TO SEND: it changes nothing when items are missing. It is NOT safe once they are all priced.

item.name: 3. Do it, with the missing prices supplied

request.description:
DESTRUCTIVE AND NOT REVERSIBLE by changing the currency back. Every key in `base_currency_prices` is `"<item_type>-<item_id>"`, and every item the preview listed under `missing` must appear or the change is refused again.

A list of `{item_type, item_id, price}` works too, as does either shape JSON-encoded as a string - which is what the dashboard sends, since this endpoint stores strings.

It is consumed by the change and never stored as a setting. Zero is accepted (an item given away on purpose); a negative number is not a price.

On success: `base_currency_change` with `adopted_from_stored` and `adopted_from_entered`.

item.name: What the base currency is right now

request.description: `base_currency` on this response is the setting, and `currency` is what THIS request is being priced in. They differ whenever a country price applies.

item.name: Upload
item.description: The general file upload, and the token it now requires.

formdata.description: Pick a file in Postman. Any role's token works.

request.description:
**BREAKING in update-16: this now needs a token.**

It used to take a file from anybody at all - no token, no role - write it to the server's disk and hand back the URL it is served from. That is free hosting on this domain for whatever a stranger wants to put there, and it was the only unguarded write on the API.

It is guarded by `anyAuthMiddleware`, the same guard `/upload/audio` already used, which accepts ANY of the four roles. Every signed-in caller keeps working unchanged; only anonymous requests are refused.

Returns `file_path` (what to store on a row) and `file_url` (the absolute URL). Send the file as a multipart part, or as a base64 data URI in the body.

What the change actually does. Before update-16 this wrote the file and returned its URL; now it is refused.

If it still succeeds, the server has not pulled the guard yet.
